title: How to tell if your laptop needs repair or replacement
metaDescription: A slow laptop isn't always a dead laptop. How to diagnose whether a repair is worth it — and when replacing it is the honest answer.
excerpt: A slow laptop isn't always a dead laptop. Here's how to diagnose whether a repair is worth it — and when replacing it is the honest answer.

body.text: A slow laptop is not automatically a broken laptop, and a broken laptop is not automatically a dead one. Most people bring a machine in expecting the worst, and most of the time it's a fixable problem — a failing drive, a clogged fan, or an operating system that just needs a clean install. If you're in the Eastern Cape and want a second opinion before you spend money on a new machine, [our IT support team](/troubleshoot) can diagnose it properly instead of guessing.

body.heading: Not sure which it is?
body.text: LYNX offers fixed-price diagnostics across the Eastern Cape. You'll know the cost before we touch anything.
A repair makes sense when the cost is well under half the price of a comparable new machine, and when the rest of the hardware is still healthy.

items: **It's slow, not dead.** A sluggish machine with a working screen and keyboard is almost always a software or storage problem.
**The fan is loud or the laptop is hot.** That's dust and dried thermal paste — a cheap, fast fix that buys years.
**It won't boot, but the drive spins up.** Often a corrupted OS or a failing drive. Both are replaceable.
**The battery dies fast.** Batteries are consumables. Replacing one on a good laptop is almost always worth it.

body.text: Replacement is the honest answer when the repair cost starts approaching the price of something newer and faster.

items: **The motherboard has failed.** On older machines, motherboard replacement is often more expensive than the laptop is worth.
**The screen is cracked and the chassis is warped.** When two or three major components fail at once, you're rebuilding, not repairing.
**It's more than six or seven years old.** New low-end laptops now out-perform mid-range machines from a decade ago.
**It can't run the software you need.** Some hardware simply can't be upgraded to meet current requirements.

body.text: If the repair quote is under half the price of a comparable replacement, repair it. If it's over, replace it. If it's somewhere in between, it depends on how much you like the machine and how soon you'd want a new one anyway.

The one thing we'd always push back on is throwing a laptop away without a diagnosis. A fifteen-minute check-up costs a fraction of a new machine, and it's the only way to know which side of the line you're on.
